sections.title: Why "find nearby" is hard for a normal index

blocks.text: A B-tree indexes one dimension. A query like "restaurants within 2 km" has two (latitude and longitude); an index on latitude alone returns a huge horizontal band of the planet that must then be filtered by longitude. Geospatial indexes map 2-D space onto structures that keep nearby points near each other in the index.

Geohash recursively halves the world: the first bit says east/west of the prime meridian, the next north/south of the equator, and so on, interleaving longitude and latitude bits. Groups of 5 bits become base-32 characters. Points that share a longer prefix are (usually) closer together, so "nearby" becomes a **prefix query** on an ordinary string index.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Querying only the user's own cell. A point just across a cell boundary is close but has a completely different prefix — always include the 8 neighbouring cells, then filter by real distance.

A quadtree splits a region into four quadrants, and keeps splitting any quadrant holding more than N points (e.g. 100). Dense cities get small cells and the ocean stays one big cell, so each leaf holds a similar number of points. Search walks down to the leaf containing the user and expands to neighbouring leaves until it has enough results. Quadtrees usually live in memory and are rebuilt periodically.

cols.title: Geohash
pros: Works in any DB/KV store with string prefixes
cons: Fixed cells regardless of density; boundary effects

cols.title: Quadtree
cons: In-memory structure to build and keep updated

cols.title: S2 / H3 cells
pros: Better shapes (H3 hexagons have uniform neighbour distances)

sections.title: Query flow for a nearby search

items: Drivers send locations every ~4 seconds: the index is **write-heavy**, so keep it in memory (Redis GEO, or an in-memory grid per city) rather than rebuilding a tree.
Update = remove from the old cell, add to the new one; expire entries that stop reporting.
Shard by city / region; matching runs against the current cell and its neighbours.
Persist location history asynchronously to a stream / time-series store.

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: For static places I'd use geohash cells plus neighbours in a read-replicated index; for drivers that move every few seconds I'd keep an in-memory grid per city in Redis and update it on every ping.
